title: Metallic bonding and comparing structures; Giant covalent structures
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BD06#t4 term and clue written for the game; BD06#t3 term and clue written for the game; BD05#t4 term and clue written for the game; BD05#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BD05#N.7, BD06#N.3a, BD05#N.10, BD06#N.11, BD05#N.11a, BD06#N.15.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ductile
items.clue: Able to be drawn into wires, because layers of ions slide.

items.label: Malleable
items.clue: Able to be hammered into shape, because layers of ions slide.

items.label: Fullerenes
items.clue: Closed cages of C atoms, such as C₆₀, that exist as separate molecules.

items.label: Graphene
items.clue: A single sheet one atom thick that conducts and is very strong for its mass.

questions.stem: Substance X melts at 1710 °C. It does not conduct electricity, either as a solid or when molten. It does not dissolve in water or in hexane. Which structure does X have?

options.text: A lattice of oppositely charged ions
A network of atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout
A lattice of metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons
Separate small molecules with very strong forces between them

questions.explanation: The very high melting point means strong bonds break. No conduction even when molten means no ions and no delocalised electrons. Insoluble everywhere: a covalent network.

questions.stem: Aluminium is rolled into kitchen foil less than 0.02 mm thick without cracking. Which statement explains this property of aluminium?

options.text: Its layers of cations slide, staying attracted to the delocalised electrons around them.
Its metallic bonds are weak, so the rollers can easily push its atoms apart.
Its bonds between neighbouring atoms bend like hinges instead of breaking.
Its individual atoms are soft, so each one is flattened as it passes between the rollers.

questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is non-directional, so the delocalised electrons keep attracting the cations after the layers have slid. The metal changes shape without cracking.

questions.stem: Hexagonal boron nitride has a layered structure like graphite, but it does not conduct electricity. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its spare electrons are held on the more electronegative N atoms, so they cannot move along the layers.
Its layers are much further apart than in graphite, so electrons cannot pass from one to the next.
It is made of B³⁺ and N³⁻ ions, which are held in fixed positions in the solid.
Each atom forms four covalent bonds, so no electrons are left over to carry a current.

questions.explanation: In graphite the fourth electron of each C is delocalised across the layer. In hexagonal BN the electron density stays on N, so no charge carriers move.

questions.stem: Four solids, P, Q, R and S, are tested. - P: melts at 801 °C; conducts when molten but not as a solid; dissolves in water. - Q: melts at 1085 °C; conducts as a solid and when molten; insoluble in water. - R: melts at 114 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water. - S: melts at 1710 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water. Which pairing of substance and structure is correct?

options.text: P is metallic, because it conducts when molten.
Q is ionic, because it conducts when molten.
R is molecular, because it melts low and never conducts.
S is ionic, because its melting point is very high.

questions.stem: Graphite conducts electricity far better along its layers than at right angles to them. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its layers slide over each other, and charge is carried only in the direction they slide.
Its ions lie between the layers, so they can move only in the plane of the layers.
Each atom forms four bonds within its layer, so no electrons are left to pass between layers.
Its delocalised electrons move freely within a layer, but cannot easily cross the gap to the next.

questions.explanation: Each C bonds to three others; its fourth electron is delocalised over its own layer only. So charge flows easily along a layer, but hardly between layers.

questions.stem: Each liquid is tested with two electrodes and a bulb. Which liquid will not conduct electricity?

options.text: Molten sodium chloride at 850 °C
Liquid mercury at 20 °C
Liquid titanium(IV) chloride, TiCl₄, at 20 °C
Molten aluminium at 700 °C

questions.explanation: TiCl₄ (boils at 136 °C) is made of small covalent molecules. With no ions and no delocalised electrons, nothing carries charge, even though titanium is a metal.
